note.explanation: Plants exchange gases with their environment through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems mainly use stomata, while woody stems exchange gases through lenticels in the bark. The gases exchanged also depend on whether it is day or night.
examples: During the day, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
At night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
note.checkAnswer: During the day, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
note.simple: Plants take in and give out different gases. The main openings are stomata in leaves and young stems, and lenticels in woody stems.

note.title: Gaseous Exchange in Plants
steps: During the day, photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
During the day, respiration also happens, but leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen overall.
At night, photosynthesis does not occur, so plants take in oxygen for respiration and release carbon dioxide.
Gases pass between the environment and inner cells through the plant surface.
Leaves and young stems exchange gases through stomata; woody stems exchange gases through lenticels in the bark.

mcqs.stem: During daytime, leaves take in which gas from the environment for photosynthesis?
rationales: Correct: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, which leaves take in from the environment.
Incorrect: oxygen is released during photosynthesis and used in respiration.
Incorrect: nitrogen is not the gas identified in this section as being taken in for photosynthesis.
Incorrect: water vapour is not the gas taken in for photosynthesis in this section.

mcqs.stem: At night, when photosynthesis is not occurring, which gas do plants release as a result of respiration?
rationales: Incorrect: oxygen is taken in for respiration at night.
Correct: plants release carbon dioxide during respiration.
Incorrect: hydrogen is not identified as a gas released in this process.
Incorrect: nitrogen is not identified as a gas released in this process.

mcqs.stem: Which structures in the epidermis allow gases to move in and out of leaves and young stems?
rationales: Correct: stomata in the epidermis allow gaseous exchange in leaves and young stems.
Incorrect: lenticels allow gaseous exchange through woody stem bark.
Incorrect: root hairs are not given as the gas-exchange structures in leaves and young stems.
Incorrect: xylem vessels transport water and salts rather than exchanging gases with the environment.

mcqs.stem: Which special pores allow gaseous exchange through the bark of woody stems?
rationales: Incorrect: stomata are described as present in the epidermis of leaves and young stems.
Correct: lenticels are special pores in the bark that allow gaseous exchange.
Incorrect: the cuticle can allow gas exchange where present, but it is not the special pore in woody bark.
Incorrect: the bark itself does not allow gaseous exchange; it contains lenticels that do.

mcqs.stem: Where does gaseous exchange occur inside the plant body?
rationales: Correct: inside the body, gaseous exchange occurs between cells and air.
Incorrect: this does not describe the internal exchange stated in the section.
Incorrect: the section explains that gases exchange through lenticels in bark, not only inside bark.
Incorrect: the section does not describe gaseous exchange as occurring between xylem and phloem.

mcqs.stem: Why can gases not pass through the entire surface of a woody stem?
rationales: Incorrect: the section says gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark itself.
Correct: the bark contains lenticels, which allow gaseous exchange with the environment.
Incorrect: root hairs are not the route for gas exchange through woody stem bark.
Incorrect: phloem is not described as allowing gas exchange with the environment.

options: The plant takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
The plant takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
The plant takes in both gases and releases neither.
The plant releases both gases and takes in neither.
mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the plant's overall gaseous exchange at night?
rationales: Correct: at night, respiration continues without photosynthesis, so plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
Incorrect: this describes the daytime exchange stated in the section.
Incorrect: the section states that plants exchange gases during respiration.
Incorrect: the section states that plants take in oxygen at night.

written.text: Differentiate between: v. Lenticular transpiration and stomatal transpiration
written.finalAnswer: Stomatal transpiration is the loss of water vapour through stomata in leaves and young stems; lenticular transpiration is the loss of water vapour through lenticels in the bark of woody stems.

written.text: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants
written.finalAnswer: Plants exchange gases through their surfaces. Gases pass between the inner cells and the environment through the epidermis; the cuticle also allows gas exchange where present. In leaves and young stems, gases move in and out through stomata. In woody stems, bark contains lenticels that allow gaseous exchange. During the day, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

Inside the plant body, gaseous exchange occurs between cells and air.

example.answer: During the day, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. At night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Gas exchange changes between day and night
explain.body: During the daytime, all plant cells carry out cellular respiration while green parts also carry out photosynthesis. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. At night, photosynthesis stops, but respiration continues: plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Plant surfaces allow gases to pass
explain.body: The epidermis of roots, stems and leaves allows the exchange of gases between the inner cells and environment. The textbook states: “At some parts a thick cuticle is present over epidermis. It also allows the exchange of gases.” Inside the plant body, exchange occurs between cells and air.

explain.title: Stomata and lenticels are important openings
explain.body: In leaves and young stems, air moves in and out through stomata in the epidermis. Woody stems are covered by bark, which does not allow gaseous exchange through its entire surface. Special pores in the bark, called lenticels, allow gaseous exchange with the environment.

mistakes: Do not reverse the daytime gases: leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen during the day.
Do not say that plants take in carbon dioxide at night; without photosynthesis, respiration means they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
Do not confuse stomata with lenticels: stomata are in leaves and young stems, while lenticels are in woody stem bark.
Do not write that gases pass through the whole bark. The bark itself does not allow gaseous exchange; its lenticels do.
For the comparison question, name both the pore and the part of the plant where it occurs.
